questions.q: What does document.getElementById("title") return?
options: The one element whose id is "title", or null if there is none
An HTMLCollection of every element whose id is "title"
A NodeList containing the matching element
An array holding the matching element

why_wrong: getElementById is singular (Element, not Elements); HTMLCollections come from methods such as getElementsByClassName.
NodeLists come from querySelectorAll; getElementById hands back the element itself.
No DOM selection method returns a real array; getElementById returns one Element or null.

questions.q: Which call creates a brand-new <li> element that can later be added to the page?
questions.explain: document.createElement("li") builds a new, empty <li> element in memory. It does not appear on the page until you insert it, for example with list.append(li) or list.appendChild(li).
why_wrong: createTextNode makes a text node whose text is the two letters "li", not an element.
querySelector only finds an <li> that already exists in the page; it creates nothing.
getElementById looks up an existing element with id="li"; it does not create one.

questions.q: What does the paragraph show after the code below runs?
options: The word Hi in normal weight
questions.explain: textContent sets plain text: the string is inserted as text and never parsed as HTML, so the tags appear literally on the page. That is why textContent is the safe default for user-supplied text, while innerHTML would parse the markup.
why_wrong: That is what innerHTML would do, because innerHTML parses the string as HTML.
textContent does not strip tags; it shows them as literal characters.
Assigning to textContent replaces the element's content, so the text does appear.

questions.q: Which call, placed inside a form's submit handler, stops the browser from submitting the form?
questions.explain: Submitting the form is the browser's default action for the submit event, and preventDefault() cancels that default action. It is the usual first line of a JavaScript validation handler, so the fields can be checked before anything is sent.
why_wrong: stopPropagation() only stops the event travelling up to ancestor elements; the form still submits.
stopImmediatePropagation() also skips other listeners on the same element, but it still does not cancel the default action.
reset() clears the fields back to their initial values; it does not cancel the submission.

questions.q: Inside a click listener, what does event.target refer to?
options: The element the click actually happened on, such as the exact button clicked
The element the listener was attached to
The parent of the clicked element
questions.explain: event.target is the element where the event started: the innermost element that was clicked. It stays the same while the event bubbles up through ancestors, which is what lets one parent listener inspect event.target in event delegation.
why_wrong: That is event.currentTarget, which differs from target whenever the listener sits on an ancestor.
document is the target only for events dispatched on document itself, not for a click on a page element.
target is the clicked element itself; its parent only sees the event as it bubbles.

questions.q: Which options object, passed as the third argument to addEventListener, makes the handler run only the first time the event fires?
questions.explain: With { once: true } the browser removes the listener automatically right after its first run. For example, btn.addEventListener("click", handler, { once: true }) handles only the first click.
why_wrong: capture: true makes the listener run during the capturing phase; it still runs on every event.
passive: true promises the handler will not call preventDefault(); it does not limit how often it runs.
signal removes the listener only when controller.abort() is called, not automatically after the first run.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.code:
const pin = /^[0-9]{6}$/;
console.log(pin.test("14441"));
questions.explain: The pattern needs exactly six digits from the start (^) to the end ($) of the string, and "14441" has only five, so the match fails. test() always returns a boolean, so it logs false.
why_wrong: {6} demands exactly six digits and the anchors stop a shorter string from passing; five digits is not enough.
test() returns true or false, never the matched string.
null is what match() or exec() return when nothing matches; test() returns false instead.

questions.q: Which call creates a Date for 15 August 2026?
questions.explain: The Date constructor takes (year, monthIndex, day), and monthIndex starts at 0 for January. August is the eighth month, so its index is 8 − 1 = 7.
why_wrong: Treats months as one-indexed; index 8 is September, so this gives 15 September 2026.
Swaps day and month; the second argument is always the month index.
Uses day-month-year order; the first argument must be the year.

questions.q: For a Date that falls on a Sunday, what does getDay() return?
questions.explain: getDay() returns the day of the week as a number from 0 to 6, starting with 0 for Sunday, then 1 for Monday, up to 6 for Saturday. Do not confuse it with getDate(), which returns the day of the month (1-31).
why_wrong: Counts Sunday as day 1; in getDay() 1 means Monday.
7 is Sunday in Monday-first (ISO) numbering; getDay() never returns 7.
Counts from Monday = 0, which makes Sunday 6; in getDay() 6 is Saturday.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.explain: Web Storage keeps every value as a string, so setItem converts 5 to "5" and getItem hands back "5". To get a number back you convert it yourself, for example with Number(value).
why_wrong: localStorage does not keep numbers as numbers; the 5 was converted to a string when it was stored.
getItem returns the stored string itself; typeof would say "object" only if the key were missing and getItem returned null.
The key exists, so getItem returns its value; setItem accepted the number by converting it to a string.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.code:
const student = { name: "Asha", age: 19 };
console.log(JSON.stringify(student));
questions.explain: JSON.stringify turns a JavaScript value into a JSON string. JSON puts every key in double quotes, keeps numbers as numbers, and adds no spaces by default, giving {"name":"Asha","age":19}.
why_wrong: Unquoted keys are JavaScript object-literal syntax; JSON requires keys in double quotes.
Numbers stay numbers in JSON; stringify does not wrap 19 in quotes.
That is what you get when an object is converted with String() or joined to a string, not with JSON.stringify.

questions.q: What does a call to fetch("/data.json") return?
options: A Promise that later fulfils with a Response object
The parsed JSON data from the file
The body of the file as a string
A Response object, returned straight away
questions.explain: fetch() is asynchronous: it immediately returns a Promise, which fulfils with a Response once the server answers. Reading the body is a second step, such as response.json(), which itself returns another Promise.
why_wrong: Parsing happens only when you call response.json(), and that returns yet another Promise.
The body text comes from response.text(), which is also a Promise; fetch itself does not return it.
The network request takes time, so fetch cannot return the Response synchronously; it wraps it in a Promise.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.explain: reduce starts the accumulator at the initial value 1, then adds n * 2 for each element: 1 + 6 = 7, 7 + 10 = 17, 17 + 4 = 21. The final accumulator, 21, is what reduce returns.
why_wrong: Starts the accumulator at 0 instead of the given initial value 1 (0 + 6 + 10 + 4 = 20).
Forgets the doubling and just adds the elements to 1 (1 + 3 + 5 + 2 = 11).
Ignores both the initial value and the doubling, giving the plain sum 3 + 5 + 2 = 10.

questions.q: What does the code below log?

const result = [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => n * 2);
console.log(result);
questions.explain: forEach runs the callback for each element but always returns undefined; the callback's return values are thrown away. To collect the doubled values into a new array you would use map instead.
why_wrong: That is what map() returns; forEach discards the callback's results.
forEach does not hand back the original array either; its return value is always undefined.
6 is the last callback result (3 * 2), but forEach returns no callback result at all.

questions.q: Which of these returns a LIVE collection that updates by itself when matching elements are added to or removed from the page?
questions.explain: getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that always reflects the current DOM, so its length changes as matching elements come and go. querySelectorAll instead takes a static snapshot at the moment it is called. Liveness is why removing items inside an index-based loop over a live collection can skip elements.
why_wrong: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList, a snapshot that does not change after the call.
Array.from copies that snapshot into a plain array, which is also static.
querySelector returns a single element (or null), not a collection at all.

questions.q: The user clicks the link in the code below. What happens?

options: "link" then "box" are logged, and the page does not navigate
Only "link" is logged, and the page does not navigate

questions.q: Which of these events bubbles, so one listener on a parent <form> can handle it for every input inside (event delegation)?
questions.explain: focus, blur and mouseenter do not bubble, so a listener on an ancestor never receives them on the way up. focusin (and focusout) are the bubbling versions of focus and blur, which makes them the right choice for delegation.
why_wrong: focus does not bubble; its bubbling counterpart is focusin.
blur does not bubble; its bubbling counterpart is focusout.
mouseenter does not bubble; its bubbling counterpart is mouseover.

questions.explain: ^ and $ anchor the match to the whole string, and \d{10} demands exactly ten digit characters. Only "9876543210" is ten digits with nothing else before, between or after them.
why_wrong: The space is not a digit, and the anchors do not allow any extra character.
The + sign is not a digit, and with the country code the string has 12 digits.
Only nine digits; {10} needs exactly ten.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.code:
const d = new Date(2026, 0, 32);
console.log(d.getMonth(), d.getDate());
questions.explain: January has 31 days, so day 32 of January rolls over to 1 February 2026; Date adjusts out-of-range values instead of rejecting them. getMonth() is zero-indexed, so February gives 1, and getDate() gives the day of the month, 1.
why_wrong: Date does not keep an out-of-range day; it rolls it over into the next month.
Gets the rollover right but reads getMonth() as one-indexed; February is 1, not 2.
An out-of-range day does not make an invalid date; the value is rolled over, not rejected.

questions.q: Which statement about the Web Storage API is NOT true?
options: sessionStorage data is shared by every tab open on the same site
localStorage data is still there after the browser is closed and reopened
Every stored value is a string, so objects are saved with JSON.stringify
localStorage data is not sent to the server with each HTTP request
questions.explain: sessionStorage is scoped to a single tab: each tab has its own copy, and it is cleared when that tab is closed. The other three statements are true: localStorage persists until code or the user clears it, all values are strings, and unlike cookies, Web Storage is never attached to HTTP requests.
why_wrong: This is true: localStorage has no expiry and survives closing the browser.
This is true: setItem converts values to strings, so objects need JSON.stringify to save and JSON.parse to read back.
This is true: cookies travel with requests, but Web Storage stays in the browser.

The Promise rejects only on network-level failures, such as no connection.
why_wrong: Assumes fetch rejects on HTTP error statuses; it rejects only when the request fails at the network level.
res.ok is true only for statuses 200-299, so a 404 gives false.
The .then did not throw, so the chain never reaches .catch.

questions.q: A results page must show the names, in capitals, of students who scored 40 or more. Using the students array in the code below, which expression gives ["ASHA", "MEENA"]?

The order matters: after map runs, the elements are plain strings with no marks property. An arrow body in braces must say return, or the callback returns undefined.
why_wrong: map runs first and produces strings. A string has no marks property, so s.marks >= 40 becomes undefined >= 40, which is false, and the result is [].
forEach always returns undefined, so calling .map on its result throws a TypeError.

questions.q: In a to-do app, the code below moves task X from the Pending list to the Done list. Because of a bug, the append line runs twice. What is logged?

The first append takes X out of #pending and puts it in #done. The second append just moves it to the same last spot in #done, so #pending has 0 children and #done has 1.

Knows the first append moves X but thinks the second append adds another copy.

questions.q: A student reports that "Hello" appears in the console as soon as the page loads, and clicking Greet afterwards does nothing. Which explanation fits the code below?
questions.code:
<button id="greet">Greet</button>
<script>
  function showMsg() {
    console.log("Hello");
  }
  document.getElementById("greet").addEventListener("click", showMsg());
</script>
options: showMsg() is called right away, and its return value (undefined) is what gets registered, so no function is attached to the click
addEventListener fires the event once when it is registered, and then the listener removes itself
The script runs before the button exists, so the listener is attached to null
A click listener only responds to mouse clicks when it is registered with the capture flag set to true
questions.explain: Writing showMsg() with brackets calls the function immediately, which logs "Hello" while the page loads. addEventListener receives the result of that call, undefined, and silently registers nothing. Passing the function itself, addEventListener("click", showMsg), hands the browser a callback to run later on every click.
why_wrong: Registering a listener never dispatches the event. The early "Hello" comes from the brackets calling the function.
The script comes after the button, so getElementById finds it. Calling addEventListener on null would throw a TypeError, not log Hello.
The capture flag only decides which phase a listener runs in. Ordinary bubbling listeners respond to clicks perfectly well.

questions.q: A custom video player has a progress bar that must move steadily while the video plays, based on video.currentTime. Which media event should the update code listen for?
questions.explain: timeupdate fires again and again while the playback position (currentTime) changes, so it is the natural hook for a progress bar. progress is about downloading: it reports that the browser is fetching more of the media file. play and ended each fire once, at the start and at the end of playback.
why_wrong: progress tracks how much of the file has been downloaded or buffered, not the playback position, and the two can be far apart.
play fires once when playback starts or resumes, so the bar would move only at that moment.
ended fires once when playback finishes, which is too late to show progress.

questions.q: A delivery form checks a 6-digit Indian PIN code with pin.test(value). The check must accept "144411" and reject both "1234567" and "LPU144411". Which pattern does that?
questions.explain: Without anchors, test() returns true if the pattern matches ANYWHERE in the string. ^ pins the match to the start and $ pins it to the end, so /^\d{6}$/ accepts only a string that is exactly six digits. "144411" passes, while "1234567" (seven digits) and "LPU144411" (letters first) both fail.
why_wrong: No anchors, so it finds six digits inside both "1234567" and "LPU144411", and both wrongly pass.
Anchored only at the start: "1234567" begins with six digits, so it wrongly passes.
Anchored only at the end: "1234567" and "LPU144411" both end with six digits, so both wrongly pass.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.explain: Date months are zero-indexed, so month 1 is February and month 2 is March. Subtracting two Dates gives the gap in milliseconds, and dividing by 1000 · 60 · 60 · 24 = 86,400,000 turns it into days. 2026 is not a leap year, so 1 February to 1 March is 28 days.
why_wrong: Reads the months as one-indexed (1 = January, 2 = February), so it counts January's 31 days.
Treats 2026 as a leap year. 2026 is not divisible by 4, so February has 28 days.
Assumes Dates cannot be subtracted. The minus operator converts each Date to its millisecond timestamp.

questions.q: The server answers the request in the code below with status 200 and the body {"total": 88}. What is logged, and why?
options: 88, because res.json() parses the body into an object
undefined, because res.json() returns a Promise, and a Promise has no total property
88, but only after a short delay, because console.log waits for the Promise to settle
A TypeError, because json() cannot be called until the body has finished downloading
questions.explain: fetch() resolves to a Response once the headers arrive. Reading the body is a second asynchronous step, so res.json() returns another Promise that later fulfils with the parsed object. Here data is that Promise, so data.total is undefined. The fix is to return res.json() and read total in the next .then (or use await res.json()).
why_wrong: Treats res.json() as returning the parsed object directly. It returns a Promise for that object.
Reading a property never waits for a Promise. data.total is read immediately, on the Promise object itself.
json() can be called as soon as the Response exists. It is exactly the method that waits for the body and parses it.

questions.q: On a quiz site, clicking Start runs the code below in Tab 1. The user then (i) reloads Tab 1, and (ii) opens a new tab, types the same site address and loads the page. What does sessionStorage.getItem("attempt") return in each?
questions.code: sessionStorage.setItem("attempt", 1);
options: Tab 1 after reload: "1"; new tab: null
Tab 1 after reload: null; new tab: null
Tab 1 after reload: 1 (a number); new tab: null
questions.explain: sessionStorage belongs to one tab: it survives reloads of that tab and is cleared when the tab closes. A tab opened fresh starts with its own empty sessionStorage, so getItem returns null there. Web Storage always stores strings, so the number 1 comes back as the string "1". Sharing between tabs of the same site is what localStorage does.
why_wrong: Thinks a reload ends the session. sessionStorage lasts until the tab is closed.
Treats sessionStorage like localStorage, which every tab of the same origin shares.
Web Storage turns every value into a string on setItem, so the number 1 comes back as "1".

questions.q: On an HTTPS page where the user has already allowed location access, the code below runs. What does the last line print?
options: Latitude: followed by the user's real latitude, because permission was already granted
Latitude: undefined, because lat is reset while the position is being looked up
A ReferenceError, because pos is not defined outside the callback

The console.log line runs before that callback, while lat still holds "unknown". Code that needs pos.coords.latitude must go inside the callback.
why_wrong: Permission removes the prompt but not the wait. The callback still runs later, after console.log.
Nothing assigns undefined to lat. It keeps "unknown" until the callback runs.
The last line reads only lat, never pos, so nothing can throw.

questions.q: The code below is meant to remove every finished task. Which items are still on the page after it runs?

questions.explain: getElementsByClassName returns a LIVE HTMLCollection, which shrinks the moment an item leaves the page. i = 0 removes A, and the collection becomes [B, C, D]. i = 1 then removes C, leaving [B, D]. Now i = 2 is not less than the length 2, so the loop stops. Looping backwards, or using the static NodeList from querySelectorAll, would remove all four.
why_wrong: Treats the collection as a fixed snapshot. That is how querySelectorAll's NodeList behaves, not getElementsByClassName's collection.
Assumes the loop removed the first two items (A and B), ignoring that the indexes shift after each removal.
Gets the skipping right but reverses it: A and C are the items removed, not the ones left.

questions.q: The code below runs, and then the user clicks the Like button. What is logged?
options: Nothing, because the Like button on screen is a new element with no listener
"liked" twice, because the listener is copied along with the new content
A TypeError, because the variable like now points to a removed element
questions.explain: box.innerHTML += ... means box.innerHTML = box.innerHTML + ...: it reads the box as an HTML string, throws away every child element, and builds new ones from that string. Listeners are not part of HTML text, so the new Like button has none. The old button, still held in the variable like, keeps its listener but is no longer on the page. Adding the paragraph with createElement and append would keep the original button.
why_wrong: Assumes += only adds the new paragraph. In fact the whole contents are re-parsed and the original button is replaced.
Listeners belong to element objects, not to the HTML string, so nothing is copied, let alone duplicated.
Nothing reads the variable like after the click. The detached button just sits unused, so no error is thrown.

questions.q: The user clicks Go in the code below. What is logged?
questions.explain: The outer listener is registered with capture = true, so it runs on the way down, before the event reaches the button. stopPropagation() halts the event right there: it never reaches the target and never bubbles back up, so the btn and document listeners do not run. stopPropagation stops the event in whichever phase it is called, not only during bubbling.
why_wrong: Thinks stopPropagation only blocks bubbling above outer, so the target's own listener would still run.
Ignores the capture flag and treats outer as a bubbling listener that runs after btn.
Thinks stopPropagation has no effect when called in the capturing phase, so the event finishes normally.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.code:
<button id="btn">Go</button>
<script>
  const btn = document.getElementById("btn");
  const controller = new AbortController();
  btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("A"), { signal: controller.signal });
  btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("B"), { once: true });
  btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("C"));
  btn.click();
  controller.abort();
  btn.click();
</script>
options: A B C, then A C
A B C, then A B C
questions.explain: The first click() runs all three listeners in the order they were registered: A, B, C. once: true removes B automatically after its first run, and controller.abort() removes every listener registered with that controller's signal, which is A. The second click() therefore finds only C.
why_wrong: Assumes AbortController only cancels fetch requests. Aborting its signal also removes the listeners registered with it.
Assumes abort() removes every listener on the button. It removes only the ones registered with that signal.
Assumes neither once nor abort() removes anything. once drops B after its first run and abort() drops A, so the second click reaches only C.

questions.q: What does the code below log?
questions.code:
<input id="pin" pattern="[0-9]{6}" value="1234567">
<script>
  const pin = document.getElementById("pin");
  console.log(pin.checkValidity(), /[0-9]{6}/.test(pin.value));
</script>
questions.explain: The HTML pattern attribute must match the WHOLE value, as if it had ^ at the start and $ at the end, so seven digits break it and checkValidity() returns false. A JavaScript regex gets no such automatic anchoring: test() looks for six digits anywhere, finds "123456", and returns true. To apply the same rule in JavaScript you must write ^ and $ yourself.
why_wrong: Assumes the pattern attribute also searches anywhere in the value, like an unanchored JavaScript regex.
Assumes test() must match the whole string too. Without ^ and $ it only needs a match somewhere.
Swaps the two rules: the attribute is the one that is anchored automatically, and the JavaScript regex is not.

questions.q: The user leaves the email box empty and clicks Join. What happens with the code below?
questions.code:
<form id="signup">
  <input type="email" name="email" required>
  <button>Join</button>
</form>
<script>
  document.getElementById("signup").addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    console.log("checking in JS");
  });
</script>
options: The browser shows its built-in "fill in this field" message on the email box, and nothing is logged
"checking in JS" is logged, and then the browser shows its message
"checking in JS" is logged and no message appears, because preventDefault() also switches off the required check
The form submits and the page reloads, because a button with no type attribute does not trigger validation
questions.explain: Built-in constraint validation runs BEFORE the submit event is dispatched. The required field is empty, so the browser blocks the submission, fires an invalid event on the input and shows its message. The submit event never fires, so the handler does not run. A <button> inside a form defaults to type="submit", so clicking it does start this process.

questions.explain: By default an element refuses drops: the browser's default action for dragover means "no drop here". A drop target must call e.preventDefault() in its dragover handler to cancel that default, and only then does the drop event fire. The preventDefault() already in the drop handler cannot help, because drop never happens.
why_wrong: Cancelling dragstart stops the drag from starting at all, so Pen could not even be picked up.
The drop handler never runs, so nothing added to it can help. stopPropagation also has nothing to do with whether a drop is allowed.
draggable marks the element that can be picked up, and Pen already has it. A drop target does not need it.
